title: Foxes Hunt Better Facing One Compass Direction: 73% vs 18%

scenes.text: Foxes pounce better when they face northeast.
A red fox hears a mouse under deep snow, then leaps high and dives in headfirst.
Researchers logged nearly 600 jumps. Facing northeast, 73 percent hit their target.
Facing the opposite way, 60 percent. Any other direction, just 18.
One idea is that the fox reads Earth's magnetic field like a rangefinder.
Nobody has proven it yet. But the foxes keep leaping northeast.

description:
Foxes pounce better when they face northeast.
In a study of nearly 600 jumps, red foxes hit their hidden prey 73 percent of the time facing northeast, 60 percent facing the opposite way, and only 18 percent in any other direction. Researchers suspect the Earth's magnetic field helps them judge distance, though that is still unproven.
Would you trust a fox's compass? Comment below.
first_comment: Why northeast? Scientists still can't prove how the fox senses it. What's your guess?
